title: Cue words and self-talk
summary: Short cue words about the target can help more than slogans. How to choose two or three with your coach, and why “don't” cues can backfire.

body.html: Self-talk is what you say to yourself, aloud or in your head. A cue word is a very short instruction, such as “front edge” or “smooth”, that points your attention at one thing.

In many studies, athletes who practised what to say to themselves did somewhat better. In tasks that need accuracy, short instructions (“front edge”) helped more than encouragement (“come on”). The studies are not from clay shooting, so most likely this works in Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™ and Compak® Sporting too.

Choose two or three short cues with your coach in training. Good cues point at the target or its line: “see it”, “front edge”, “stay on the line”, “finish it”. Keep body cues, such as “elbow up”, for practice sessions.

Researchers call this an external focus: paying attention to the target or to where the gun is going, rather than to your own arms and shoulders. Many studies found that it works better. A newer review, which allowed for studies with no effect that often go unpublished, found the average advantage close to zero. So treat cues about the target as a sensible starting point, not a rule.

Say what to do, not what to avoid. In golf putting studies, players told “don't overshoot” sometimes overshot more, especially when their mind was busy with another task. In another study, such instructions led to over-correction. So try “stay on the line” rather than “don't stop the gun”.
Motivational phrases such as “come on” or “I can do this” may suit the walk between stands. On the stand, a short instruction usually fits better.
Use one cue per target and keep the same words in training and in competition. A new cue on the day is like new equipment: try it in training first. You can note your cues in your training diary.

notes.html: Translate the coach's cue the same way each time, in two or three words. If the coach says “front edge”, keep one equivalent for the whole tour, so the shooter can use it as self-talk.
On the stand, give cues about the target, not about body parts. Keep technical points for practice blocks, not for competition week.

key_points.html: Choose 2–3 short cues about the target with your coach.
Say what to do, not what to avoid: “stay on the line”, not “don't stop”.
Instructions on the stand, motivation between stands.
Keep the same cue words in training and in competition.

did_you_know.html: Many shooters say their cue word at the same step of the routine, just before the call. Then the word itself becomes part of the pre-shot routine.

quiz.explain: A short instruction about the target fits the stand; motivational phrases suit the walk between stands.

quiz.explain: In studies, “don't” instructions sometimes caused the error they named, so say what to do instead.

quiz.explain: In tasks that need accuracy, short instructions helped more than encouragement, so encouragement fits the time between stands.
